name: Air Connectivity per 1000 People
definition: A country-context indicator that expresses national air connectivity relative to population size, reported per 1,000 persons. It is taken directly from the reported air connectivity per 1,000 people figure, which scales the country's air connectivity score by its population. A higher value indicates that residents have relatively more scheduled air links per person, which typically eases logistics for fuel, spare parts and specialist staff. This describes the utility's operating environment, not utility performance.

name: Air Connectivity per Unit GDP
definition: A country-context indicator that expresses national air connectivity relative to the size of the economy, reported per unit of GDP. It is taken directly from the reported air connectivity per unit GDP figure, which scales the country's air connectivity score by gross domestic product. A higher value indicates the country is better connected by air than its economic size alone would suggest. This describes the utility's operating environment, not utility performance.
synonyms: air connectivity relative to economy size

name: IATA Air Connectivity Score
definition: A country-context indicator recording the IATA Air Connectivity Index score, a composite measure of how well a country is connected to the global air transport network. It is taken directly from the reported IATA air connectivity score, which weights available seat capacity by the size and importance of destination airports served. A higher score indicates more frequent and further-reaching air links, which matters for island utilities that depend on air freight for urgent parts and technical support. This describes the utility's operating environment, not utility performance.

name: Access to Electricity
definition: A country-context indicator measuring the share of the national population with access to electricity, expressed as a percentage. It is taken directly from the reported access-to-electricity figure, typically the proportion of the population living in electrified premises. A higher value means fewer unserved households and, for the utility, a more saturated market where growth comes from consumption rather than new connections. This describes the utility's operating environment, not utility performance, although utility grid-extension programmes influence it over time.

name: GDP per Capita
definition: A country-context indicator measuring gross domestic product per person, expressed in currency. It is taken directly from the reported GDP per capita figure, which divides national GDP by population. A higher value generally indicates greater customer affordability, higher electricity demand per household and stronger capacity to pay cost-reflective tariffs. This describes the utility's operating environment, not utility performance.

name: Inflation Rate
definition: A country-context indicator measuring the annual rate of change in consumer prices, expressed as a percentage. It is taken directly from the reported national inflation rate. Higher inflation erodes the real value of fixed tariffs and increases pressure on utility input costs such as labour, materials and fuel. This describes the utility's operating environment, not utility performance, and should be considered when comparing cost and tariff trends across years.

name: Unemployment Rate
definition: A country-context indicator measuring the share of the labour force that is unemployed, expressed as a percentage. It is taken directly from the reported national unemployment rate. A higher value signals weaker household purchasing power, which can affect electricity sales growth, arrears and disconnection rates. This describes the utility's operating environment, not utility performance.

name: USD Exchange Rate
definition: A country-context indicator recording the exchange rate between the local currency and the United States dollar, expressed as a number of local currency units per USD. It is taken directly from the reported USD exchange rate for the period. A weakening local currency (more units per USD) raises the local cost of imported fuel, plant and spare parts, which are usually priced in USD. This describes the utility's operating environment, not utility performance, and is used to convert financial KPIs to a common currency for regional comparison.

name: Fuel Pricing Regulation
definition: A country-context descriptor recording how fuel prices are regulated in the country; it is categorical and has no numeric unit. It is taken directly from the reported fuel pricing regulation entry, which describes whether and how government or a regulator controls fuel prices. Regulated fuel pricing can dampen or delay the pass-through of world oil price movements into utility generation costs and tariffs. This describes the utility's operating environment, not utility performance.

name: Fuel Supply Access
definition: A country-context descriptor recording how the country and utility access fuel supplies; it is categorical and has no numeric unit. It is taken directly from the reported fuel supply access entry, which typically covers supply arrangements, import routes and any constraints on fuel availability. Constrained or long supply chains increase fuel security risk and holding costs for diesel-dependent island utilities. This describes the utility's operating environment, not utility performance.

name: Islands
definition: A country-context indicator recording the number of islands in the country, expressed as a count. It is taken directly from the reported islands figure. A higher number of islands generally implies more dispersed, fragmented service territories with separate island grids, higher logistics costs and duplicated generation assets. This describes the utility's operating environment, not utility performance, and is important context when comparing cost and reliability KPIs across utilities.

name: Land Area
definition: A country-context indicator recording the total land area of the country, expressed in square kilometres (km2). It is taken directly from the reported land area figure. Larger or more dispersed land areas typically mean longer network lengths per customer and higher delivery costs, while very small land areas concentrate demand. This describes the utility's operating environment, not utility performance.

name: Average Household Size
definition: A country-context indicator measuring the average number of persons per household. It is taken directly from the reported average household size, which is typically national population divided by the number of households. Larger households tend to consume more electricity per connection, which affects per-customer consumption comparisons between countries. This describes the utility's operating environment, not utility performance.

name: Households
definition: A country-context indicator recording the total number of households in the country, expressed as a count. It is taken directly from the reported households figure, usually from census or national statistics. It indicates the potential residential customer base and, compared against customer counts, helps gauge remaining electrification headroom. This describes the utility's operating environment, not utility performance.

name: Population
definition: A country-context indicator recording the total national population, expressed in persons. It is taken directly from the reported population figure, usually from census or national statistics. Population is the key scaling denominator for per-capita comparisons across utilities of very different sizes. This describes the utility's operating environment, not utility performance.

name: Rural Population
definition: A country-context indicator measuring the share of the national population living in rural areas, expressed as a percentage. It is taken directly from the reported rural population percentage. A higher rural share generally implies more dispersed demand, longer distribution lines per customer and higher costs to serve. This describes the utility's operating environment, not utility performance.

name: Urban Population
definition: A country-context indicator measuring the share of the national population living in urban areas, expressed as a percentage. It is taken directly from the reported urban population percentage. A higher urban share generally means denser, cheaper-to-serve demand concentrated around main centres. This describes the utility's operating environment, not utility performance.

name: Accounting Standards
definition: A utility-context descriptor recording which accounting standards the utility follows in preparing its financial statements; it is categorical and has no numeric unit. It is taken directly from the reported accounting standards entry, for example IFRS or a national equivalent. Knowing the standard in use matters when comparing financial KPIs, because measurement of items such as depreciation, revaluation and provisions differs between frameworks. This describes reporting context, not utility performance.

name: Electricity Regulation
definition: A country-context descriptor recording how the electricity sector is regulated in the country; it is categorical and has no numeric unit. It is taken directly from the reported electricity regulation entry, typically covering whether an independent regulator exists and how tariffs are set. The regulatory regime shapes tariff levels, cost recovery and investment incentives, so it is essential context for financial and tariff comparisons. This describes the utility's operating environment, not utility performance.

name: Feeder Type
definition: A utility-context descriptor recording the predominant type of distribution feeders operated by the utility; it is categorical and has no numeric unit. It is taken directly from the reported feeder type entry, typically distinguishing overhead from underground construction. Feeder type strongly influences fault exposure and reliability results, since overhead lines are more vulnerable to weather, vegetation and salt spray, while underground cables cost more but fail less often. This is context for interpreting reliability and cost KPIs, not a performance measure in itself.

name: Ownership Type
definition: A utility-context descriptor recording the ownership structure of the utility; it is categorical and has no numeric unit. It is taken directly from the reported entity ownership type, for example state-owned enterprise, government department, private company or cooperative. Ownership shapes governance, commercial incentives and access to capital, and is useful context when comparing efficiency and financial KPIs across utilities. This describes the utility's institutional setting, not its performance.

name: Power Quality Standards
definition: A utility-context descriptor recording which power quality standards the utility applies, such as voltage and frequency limits; it is categorical and has no numeric unit. It is taken directly from the reported power quality standards entry. The standards in force determine what counts as acceptable supply quality and therefore affect how reliability and quality-of-supply results should be compared between utilities. This is context for interpretation, not a performance measure in itself.

name: Duty on Fuel and Lube Oil
definition: Measures import duty and taxes levied on fuel and lubricating oil as a share of the utility's cost base, expressed as a percentage. It is sourced directly from the utility-reported apportioned cost of duty and taxes on fuel and lubricating oil, presented alongside the other cost-breakdown categories. A high share indicates that government fiscal charges on fuel imports form a material part of the cost of supply, which the utility cannot reduce through operational efficiency. For diesel-dependent Pacific utilities, changes in national duty policy can move this figure independently of any change in utility performance.
synonyms: Fuel and lubricant duties and taxes

name: Fuel Expenditure
definition: Measures spending on fuel and oil as a proportion of the utility's total costs, expressed as a percentage. Calculated as fuel and oil operating costs divided by total service costs. A high share signals heavy exposure to imported fuel prices, which is typical of diesel-dependent Pacific systems, while a falling share often reflects growing renewable generation or lower world fuel prices rather than cost control. Because fuel is purchased in foreign currency, exchange-rate movements can shift this ratio independently of operational performance.
synonyms: Fuel cost as a share of total costs

name: Generation Labor Costs
definition: Measures the cost of the generation function as a share of the utility's total costs, expressed as a percentage. In the current formula it is calculated as generation operations and maintenance costs divided by total service costs. A high share points to a cost structure dominated by power production, while a low share suggests costs sit mainly in networks, retail or overheads. Comparisons across utilities should allow for differences in generation mix, since diesel-heavy fleets carry structurally higher generation costs than hydro or solar systems.

name: Generation O&M Costs
definition: Measures generation operations and maintenance spending as a proportion of the utility's total costs, expressed as a percentage. Calculated as generation O&M costs divided by total service costs. A high share indicates that running and maintaining power stations dominates the cost base, which may reflect an ageing or diesel-heavy fleet; a low share suggests costs are concentrated in networks or overheads. Differences in generation mix and plant age mean this ratio should be read alongside fuel expenditure rather than in isolation.

name: Other Duty and Taxes
definition: Measures duty and taxes other than those on fuel and lubricating oil as a share of the utility's total costs, expressed as a percentage. Calculated as apportioned other duty and taxes divided by total service costs. A high share indicates that government fiscal charges beyond fuel duties form a material part of the cost of supply. These charges are set by government policy rather than utility management, so they reflect the fiscal environment more than operating efficiency.
synonyms: Other fiscal charges share of costs

name: Other Expenditure
definition: Measures other operating expenses as a proportion of the utility's total costs, expressed as a percentage. Calculated as other operating expenses divided by total service costs. A high share can indicate significant administrative, insurance or miscellaneous costs that are not captured in the fuel, labour or O&M categories, and may warrant closer scrutiny of overheads. Inconsistent classification of costs between utilities can distort cross-utility comparison of this residual category.

name: Other Labor Expenditure
definition: Measures labour costs outside the core generation, transmission and distribution functions as a share of the utility's total costs, expressed as a percentage. Calculated as other labour expenditure divided by total service costs. A high share suggests a large administrative or support workforce relative to the technical front line, which can indicate overstaffing in overhead functions. Small Pacific utilities often carry proportionally higher support-staff costs because fixed corporate functions are spread over a small customer base.

name: Power Purchase Costs
definition: Measures the cost of electricity purchased from third parties, such as independent power producers, as a share of the utility's total costs, expressed as a percentage. Calculated as power purchase costs divided by total service costs. A rising share typically reflects growing reliance on IPPs or rooftop-solar buy-back arrangements rather than own generation, and shifts cost exposure from fuel markets to contract terms. The ratio says nothing about whether purchased power is cheaper or dearer than self-generation, so it should be read alongside generation cost KPIs.
synonyms: Power purchase share of total costs

name: Transmission and Distribution Labor Costs
definition: Measures the labour cost of the network functions as a share of the utility's total costs, expressed as a percentage. Calculated as the sum of transmission staff costs and distribution staff costs divided by total service costs. A high share indicates a labour-intensive network operation, which may reflect dispersed island grids that require large field crews, while a very low share could signal under-resourced maintenance. Geography drives much of the variation across Pacific utilities, so like-for-like comparison should consider network length and island dispersion.

name: Transmission and Distribution O&M Costs
definition: Measures operations and maintenance spending on the transmission and distribution networks as a proportion of the utility's total costs, expressed as a percentage. Calculated as the sum of transmission O&M costs and distribution O&M costs divided by total service costs. A high share indicates that network upkeep dominates the cost base, while a persistently low share may point to deferred maintenance that later surfaces as reliability problems. Cyclone exposure and salt-air corrosion mean Pacific networks often require structurally higher maintenance spending than continental systems.

name: Operating Cost Covered by Subsidies
definition: Measures how much of the utility's operating cost base is funded by government subsidies, expressed as a percentage. Calculated as government subsidies received divided by the sum of cost of sales and other operating expenses, less bad debt expense, plus income tax. A high percentage indicates heavy dependence on government support to keep operating, while a figure near zero indicates the utility funds its operations from its own revenue. Subsidies can mask poor cost recovery or below-cost tariffs, so this KPI should be read together with Operating Cost Recovery when judging financial sustainability.
synonyms: Government subsidy coverage of operating costs

name: Operating Cost Recovery
definition: Measures the extent to which revenue from operations covers the utility's operating costs, expressed as a percentage. Calculated as service revenue divided by the sum of cost of sales and other operating expenses, less bad debt expense, plus income tax. A value at or above 100% means tariff and other operating revenue fully covers operating costs, while a value below 100% signals dependence on subsidies or borrowing to sustain operations. For Pacific state-owned utilities, sustained below-100% recovery usually reflects tariffs set below cost rather than short-term cost shocks.

name: Operating Ratio
definition: Measures operating expenses as a percentage of operating revenue, indicating how much of each unit of revenue is absorbed by the cost of operations. Calculated as the sum of cost of sales and other operating expenses divided by service revenue. Lower is better: a ratio below 100% means the utility earns more from operations than it spends, and the PPA target is 70% against a Pacific regional average of 78%. Because many Pacific utilities operate under regulated tariffs and receive government support, a favourable ratio can reflect subsidised inputs or recent tariff resets as much as underlying efficiency.

name: Current Ratio
definition: Measures the utility's short-term liquidity, expressed as a ratio of what it owns to what it owes within the year. Calculated as total current assets divided by total current liabilities. A ratio above 1.0 indicates the utility can meet its near-term obligations from near-term resources, while a ratio below 1.0 signals potential cash-flow stress; a very high ratio may indicate idle cash or slow-moving inventory. For Pacific utilities, large fuel stock holdings and overdue government receivables can inflate current assets without genuinely improving liquidity.

name: Debtor Days
definition: Measures the average number of days the utility takes to collect payment from its customers after billing. Calculated as trade receivables divided by service revenue, multiplied by 365. A low figure indicates effective billing and collection, while a high figure ties up working capital and increases bad-debt risk; utilities typically aim for collection within one to two billing cycles. In the Pacific, unpaid government and state-agency accounts are a common driver of high debtor days, so the figure can reflect public-sector payment discipline as much as the utility's own collection effort.

name: EBITDA Margin
definition: Measures earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation as a percentage of revenue, indicating the cash-generating capacity of core operations. Calculated as service revenue less other income, cost of sales and other operating expenses, divided by service revenue. A higher margin means more revenue is retained after cash operating costs and is available to fund debt service, tax and capital investment; a low or negative margin signals that tariffs are not covering day-to-day operating costs. Because it excludes depreciation, a healthy EBITDA margin can coexist with an inability to fund asset replacement, which matters for capital-hungry island grids.

name: EBIT Margin
formula: ( service_revenue + service_other_income - service_cost_of_sales - service_other_operating_expenses - service_depreciation_expense - service_amortization_expenses ) / service_revenue
definition: Measures earnings before interest and tax as a percentage of revenue, showing operating profitability after the cost of consuming assets. Calculated as service revenue plus other income, less cost of sales, other operating expenses, depreciation and amortisation, divided by service revenue. A higher margin indicates operations generate a genuine surplus after providing for asset wear, while a negative margin means tariffs do not cover the full economic cost of supply. Where asset registers are outdated or assets are grant-funded, understated depreciation can flatter this margin for Pacific utilities.

name: Profit Margin
definition: Measures net profit as a percentage of revenue, showing how much of each unit of revenue remains after all costs. Calculated as service profit divided by service revenue. A positive margin indicates the utility is financially self-sustaining and able to fund reinvestment, while a persistent negative margin signals reliance on government support or accumulating losses. Government subsidies and community service obligations can distort the margin for Pacific state-owned utilities, so it should be read alongside the subsidy-coverage KPIs.

name: Return on Assets
definition: Measures how effectively the utility uses its asset base to generate profit, expressed as a percentage. Calculated as service profit divided by total assets. A higher return indicates assets are being worked productively, while a low or negative return suggests underused capacity, below-cost tariffs or an inflated asset base. Grant-funded and donor-funded assets are common in the Pacific and enlarge the denominator without a matching revenue obligation, which can depress reported returns relative to utilities that debt-fund their assets.

name: Return on Equity
definition: Measures the profit generated on the owners' investment in the utility, expressed as a percentage. Calculated as service profit divided by total equity. A higher return indicates the utility is creating value for its shareholder, typically the government for Pacific utilities, while a low or negative return means the owner's capital is being eroded. Because equity can be distorted by asset revaluations, accumulated losses or government capital injections, the ratio should be interpreted alongside return on assets and gearing.

name: Customer Sales
definition: Measures the utility's total revenue from the sale of electricity services to customers, expressed in local currency. It is taken directly from reported service revenue rather than derived from other inputs. Growth in customer sales reflects some combination of tariff levels, customer numbers and consumption, so it indicates scale rather than efficiency or profitability. Local-currency reporting means cross-utility comparison requires conversion at consistent exchange rates and is sensitive to inflation.

name: Debt to Equity Ratio
definition: Measures the utility's financial leverage, expressed as a ratio of what it owes to the owners' stake in the business. Calculated as total liabilities divided by total equity, a broader basis than definitions that use interest-bearing debt only. A higher ratio indicates greater reliance on borrowed or owed funds and higher financial risk, while a low ratio indicates a conservatively funded balance sheet with headroom to borrow for capital works. For Pacific state-owned utilities, concessional and government-guaranteed loans can make high gearing less risky than the raw ratio suggests.

name: 10,000 kWh
definition: Reports the amount a customer would be billed for consuming 10,000 kWh in a period under the utility's prevailing tariff, expressed in local currency at service-area level. It is compiled from the utility's published tariff structure rather than calculated from a formula, and represents a large commercial or industrial consumption level. Comparing billed amounts at standard consumption points shows how tariff design treats large consumers, who often cross-subsidise smaller users. As a regulated local-currency price it reflects tariff policy and subsidy settings rather than utility efficiency, and cross-utility comparison requires currency conversion.

name: 1,000 kWh
definition: Reports the amount a customer would be billed for consuming 1,000 kWh in a period under the utility's prevailing tariff, expressed in local currency at service-area level. It is compiled from the utility's published tariff structure rather than calculated from a formula, and represents a large household or small commercial consumption level. Comparing billed amounts at standard consumption points allows tariff levels and block structures to be benchmarked across utilities. As a regulated local-currency price it reflects tariff policy and subsidy settings rather than utility efficiency, and cross-utility comparison requires currency conversion.

name: 100 kWh
definition: Reports the amount a customer would be billed for consuming 100 kWh in a period under the utility's prevailing tariff, expressed in local currency at service-area level. It is compiled from the utility's published tariff structure rather than calculated from a formula, and represents a low-consumption household. Comparing billed amounts at standard consumption points shows how affordable basic electricity use is under each utility's tariff design. As a regulated local-currency price it reflects tariff policy and subsidy settings rather than utility efficiency, and cross-utility comparison requires currency conversion.

name: 200 kWh
definition: Reports the amount a customer would be billed for consuming 200 kWh in a period under the utility's prevailing tariff, expressed in local currency at service-area level. It is compiled from the utility's published tariff structure rather than calculated from a formula, and represents a typical household consumption level in many Pacific markets. Comparing billed amounts at standard consumption points allows residential tariff levels to be benchmarked across the region. As a regulated local-currency price it reflects tariff policy and subsidy settings rather than utility efficiency, and cross-utility comparison requires currency conversion.

name: 5,000 kWh
definition: Reports the amount a customer would be billed for consuming 5,000 kWh in a period under the utility's prevailing tariff, expressed in local currency at service-area level. It is compiled from the utility's published tariff structure rather than calculated from a formula, and represents a commercial-scale consumption level. Comparing billed amounts at standard consumption points shows how tariff design treats business consumers relative to households. As a regulated local-currency price it reflects tariff policy and subsidy settings rather than utility efficiency, and cross-utility comparison requires currency conversion.

name: 500 kWh
definition: Reports the amount a customer would be billed for consuming 500 kWh in a period under the utility's prevailing tariff, expressed in local currency at service-area level. It is compiled from the utility's published tariff structure rather than calculated from a formula, and represents a high-consumption household or very small business. Comparing billed amounts at standard consumption points allows tariff levels and block structures to be benchmarked across utilities. As a regulated local-currency price it reflects tariff policy and subsidy settings rather than utility efficiency, and cross-utility comparison requires currency conversion.

name: Lifeline 120 kWh
definition: Reports the amount a customer would be billed for consuming 120 kWh in a period under the utility's lifeline tariff, the subsidised rate offered to low-consumption households, expressed in local currency at service-area level. It is compiled from the utility's published tariff structure rather than calculated from a formula. Comparing lifeline bills at standard consumption points shows how much protection each utility's tariff design gives low-income customers. Because lifeline rates are a social-policy instrument, a low figure reflects deliberate cross-subsidy or government support rather than low cost of supply.

name: Lifeline 180 kWh
definition: Reports the amount a customer would be billed for consuming 180 kWh in a period under the utility's lifeline tariff, the subsidised rate offered to low-consumption households, expressed in local currency at service-area level. It is compiled from the utility's published tariff structure rather than calculated from a formula. This point sits at the upper end of typical lifeline thresholds, so it shows how the subsidised rate tapers as household consumption approaches the standard tariff. Because lifeline rates are a social-policy instrument, a low figure reflects deliberate cross-subsidy or government support rather than low cost of supply.

name: Lifeline 60 kWh
definition: Reports the amount a customer would be billed for consuming 60 kWh in a period under the utility's lifeline tariff, the subsidised rate offered to low-consumption households, expressed in local currency at service-area level. It is compiled from the utility's published tariff structure rather than calculated from a formula. This point represents very basic electricity use, so it is the clearest indicator of affordability for the poorest connected households. Because lifeline rates are a social-policy instrument, a low figure reflects deliberate cross-subsidy or government support rather than low cost of supply.

name: Are Ministers appointed to the Board
definition: Records whether government ministers sit as directors on the utility's board, captured as a Yes/No response in the PPA governance questionnaire. It reflects the degree of separation between the state's ownership role and the utility's commercial direction. A No response is generally regarded as better practice, since direct ministerial membership can blur policy, regulatory and ownership roles and weaken the board's commercial independence. When aggregated across utilities, responses are reported as the share of participating utilities with ministers on their boards.

name: Are Ministers or public servants representing the line/sector Ministry appointed to the Board
definition: Records whether ministers or public servants from the line or sector ministry responsible for energy sit on the utility's board, captured as a Yes/No response in the PPA governance questionnaire. It reflects whether the body that sets sector policy also participates directly in the utility's governance. A No response is generally regarded as better practice, because line-ministry representation on the board can create conflicts between the ministry's policy and regulatory functions and the utility's commercial interests. When aggregated across utilities, responses are reported as the share of participating utilities with such appointments.
synonyms: Sector ministry appointees on the board

name: Is a Commercial mandate implemented
definition: Records whether the utility's commercial mandate is actually applied in practice, captured as a Yes/No response in the PPA governance questionnaire. It goes a step beyond having a mandate on paper, asking whether the utility genuinely operates on commercial principles such as cost-reflective pricing and accountability for financial results. A Yes response indicates the state-owned utility is run as a business rather than as an extension of government administration. Implementation is self-assessed, so responses may be more favourable than independent review would suggest.

name: Is a Commercial mandate in place
definition: Records whether the utility has a formal mandate to operate on commercial principles, typically set out in its establishing legislation, statement of corporate intent or ownership policy, captured as a Yes/No response in the PPA governance questionnaire. A Yes response indicates the owner has formally directed the utility to pursue commercial objectives, which underpins cost recovery and financial sustainability. Having a mandate in place does not guarantee it is followed, so this item is paired with a separate question on implementation. When aggregated across utilities, responses are reported as the share of participating utilities with a mandate in place.

name: Is a Code of Conduct implemented
definition: Records whether the utility's code of conduct is actively applied, for example through staff training, sign-off and enforcement of breaches, captured as a Yes/No response in the PPA governance questionnaire. It distinguishes utilities that operationalise their ethics framework from those where the code exists only as a document. A Yes response indicates stronger integrity practices, which support procurement discipline and reduce fraud and conflict-of-interest risk. Implementation is self-assessed, so responses reflect the utility's own judgement rather than an independent audit.

name: Is a Code of Conduct in place
definition: Records whether the utility has adopted a formal code of conduct governing the behaviour of its directors and staff, captured as a Yes/No response in the PPA governance questionnaire. A code of conduct sets expectations on ethics, conflicts of interest and use of company resources, and is a baseline element of good corporate governance. A Yes response indicates the foundation is in place, though a separate questionnaire item tests whether the code is actually implemented. When aggregated across utilities, responses are reported as the share of participating utilities with a code in place.

name: Does the CEOs performance contract include annual reviews
definition: Records whether the chief executive's performance contract provides for formal annual performance reviews, captured as a Yes/No response in the PPA governance questionnaire. Annual reviews give the board a regular, structured opportunity to hold the CEO accountable against agreed targets and to link remuneration or renewal to results. A Yes response indicates a stronger executive accountability cycle than a contract that is only assessed at expiry. The item records whether reviews are provided for, not whether they are conducted rigorously.

name: Is the CEO on a performance contract
definition: Records whether the utility's chief executive is employed under a contract with defined performance targets, captured as a Yes/No response in the PPA governance questionnaire. A performance contract links the CEO's tenure and incentives to agreed operational and financial results, giving the board a concrete accountability mechanism. A Yes response is regarded as good practice for state-owned utilities, where executive accountability can otherwise be diluted by political appointment processes. When aggregated across utilities, responses are reported as the share of participating utilities whose CEOs are on performance contracts.

name: Does the Strategic Plan include three or more years of forecasts
definition: Records whether the utility's strategic plan contains financial and operational forecasts covering at least three years, captured as a Yes/No response in the PPA governance questionnaire. Multi-year forecasting shows the utility is planning investment, tariffs and financing over a horizon that matches the long-lived nature of power assets. A Yes response indicates more mature planning than a plan limited to a single budget year. Forecast quality is not tested by this item, only whether the forward horizon exists.

name: Has a Strategic Plan been adopted
definition: Records whether the utility's board has formally adopted a strategic plan, captured as a Yes/No response in the PPA governance questionnaire. A board-adopted plan sets the utility's objectives, investment priorities and performance targets, and provides the reference point against which management and annual reports can be assessed. A Yes response indicates the basic planning discipline is in place; separate items test the plan's forecasting depth and implementation. When aggregated across utilities, responses are reported as the share of participating utilities with an adopted plan.

name: Is the Strategic Plan implemented
definition: Records whether the utility's strategic plan is actively used to direct operations and investment, captured as a Yes/No response in the PPA governance questionnaire. Implementation means the plan's targets flow into budgets, work programmes and management reporting rather than sitting on a shelf. A Yes response indicates the utility closes the loop between planning and execution, which is where many governance frameworks fail in practice. Implementation is self-assessed, so responses may overstate the plan's day-to-day influence.

name: Does the Annual Report disclose performance relative to the Strategic Plan
definition: Records whether the utility's annual report presents actual performance against the targets in its strategic plan, captured as a Yes/No response in the PPA governance questionnaire. Plan-versus-actual disclosure lets the owner, regulator and public judge whether the utility is delivering on its stated objectives, closing the accountability loop between planning and reporting. A Yes response indicates a higher standard of transparency than financial statements alone. When aggregated across utilities, responses are reported as the share of participating utilities making this disclosure.

name: Is the Annual Report audited
definition: Records whether the financial statements in the utility's annual report are subject to independent audit, captured as a Yes/No response in the PPA governance questionnaire. An external audit provides assurance that reported financial results fairly present the utility's position, which underpins the credibility of every financial KPI in the benchmarking programme. A Yes response is a baseline expectation for state-owned enterprises and lenders alike, and a No response materially weakens confidence in the utility's reported data. The item does not distinguish between clean, qualified or delayed audit opinions.

name: Is the Annual Report completed within four months of the end of the reporting year
definition: Records whether the utility completes its annual report within four months of the financial year end, captured as a Yes/No response in the PPA governance questionnaire. Timely reporting indicates disciplined financial close processes and gives the owner, lenders and regulators current information for decision-making. A Yes response reflects good practice; long delays, which are common among Pacific state-owned enterprises, reduce the usefulness of the report and often signal capacity constraints in the finance function or a backlog at the national audit office. When aggregated across utilities, responses are reported as the share of participating utilities reporting on time.

name: Administrative Employees Female %
definition: The share of the utility's administrative workforce who are women, expressed as a percentage. Calculated as the number of female administrative employees divided by the total number of administrative employees. A higher value indicates greater female representation in the division, and the KPI supports the PPA's gender-representation reporting. In small divisions the percentage can swing sharply with a single hire or departure.

name: Administrative Employees Male %
definition: The share of the utility's administrative workforce who are men, expressed as a percentage. Calculated as the number of male administrative employees divided by the total number of administrative employees. A higher value indicates greater male representation in the division; read together with the female percentage, the two shares account for the whole division. In small divisions the percentage can swing sharply with a single hire or departure.

name: Administrative Employees Total
definition: The total number of employees in the utility's administrative division, expressed as a headcount. Calculated as the sum of female and male administrative employees. Higher totals generally reflect a larger utility or a larger administrative function, so the figure is best read alongside overall workforce size and customer numbers. This is a headcount rather than a full-time-equivalent measure, so part-time staff count the same as full-time staff.

name: Employees Female %
definition: The share of the utility's total workforce who are women, expressed as a percentage. Calculated as the number of female employees divided by total employees, multiplied by 100. A higher value indicates greater female representation across the utility, and this is a headline indicator in the PPA's gender-representation reporting. At small utilities the figure can move noticeably with a handful of hires or departures.

name: Employees Male %
definition: The share of the utility's total workforce who are men, expressed as a percentage. Calculated as the number of male employees divided by total employees, multiplied by 100. A higher value indicates greater male representation; read together with the female percentage, the two shares account for the whole workforce. At small utilities the figure can move noticeably with a handful of hires or departures.

name: Executive Employees Female %
definition: The share of the utility's executive workforce who are women, expressed as a percentage. Calculated as the number of female executive employees divided by the total number of executive employees. A higher value indicates greater female representation in the division, and the KPI supports the PPA's gender-representation reporting. In small divisions the percentage can swing sharply with a single hire or departure.
synonyms: female share of executive team staff

name: Gender of Utility 2nd in command
definition: A categorical indicator recording the gender of the utility's second-in-command, typically the deputy CEO or equivalent; it has no numeric unit. Reported directly by the utility rather than calculated from other inputs. Across the region it shows female representation in the most senior deputy roles and supports the PPA's reporting on gender representation in leadership. As a single-person attribute, it changes only when the post-holder changes.

name: Gender of Utility CEO
definition: A categorical indicator recording the gender of the utility's chief executive officer; it has no numeric unit. Reported directly by the utility rather than calculated from other inputs. Across the region it shows how many Pacific utilities are led by women and supports the PPA's reporting on gender representation in senior leadership. As a single-person attribute, it changes only when the CEO changes.

name: Other Divisions Employees Total

name: Total Employees
definition: The utility's total workforce, expressed as a headcount of employees. Calculated as the sum of male and female employees. A larger workforce generally reflects a larger utility; on its own it says little about efficiency, so it is normally read alongside customer numbers and labour productivity. This is a headcount rather than a full-time-equivalent measure, so part-time staff count the same as full-time staff.

name: Total Employees Female
formula: administrative_employees_female + executive_employees_female + finance_employees_female + human_resource_employees_female + ict_employees_female + other_employees_female + pr_marketing_and_customer_service_employees_female + procurement_employees_female + technical_employees_female
definition: The total number of female employees across the utility, expressed as a headcount. Calculated as the sum of female employees across the administrative, executive, finance, human resources, ICT, other, PR/marketing/customer service, procurement and technical divisions. A higher count reflects stronger female participation in the workforce, and the figure feeds the utility-wide female percentage used in the PPA's gender-representation reporting.

name: Total Employees Male
formula: administrative_employees_male + executive_employees_male + finance_employees_male + ict_employees_male + other_employees_male + pr_marketing_and_customer_service_employees_male + procurement_employees_male + technical_employees_male
definition: The total number of male employees across the utility, expressed as a headcount. Calculated as the sum of male employees across the administrative, executive, finance, ICT, other, PR/marketing/customer service, procurement and technical divisions. A higher count simply reflects a larger male workforce and is best read alongside the female count and total headcount. Note that, as currently defined, the formula omits male human resources employees, so the figure may slightly understate the true total.

name: FTE Paid Hours - Conventional Generation
definition: The size of the utility's conventional (thermal) generation workforce expressed as full-time-equivalent (FTE) staff, based on hours paid. Calculated as total hours paid in conventional (thermal) generation divided by the standard work hours of one full-time employee, which converts paid hours into an equivalent number of full-time staff. Higher values indicate a larger paid labour input to conventional (thermal) generation. Because paid hours include annual leave, sick leave and public holidays, this measure normally sits above the corresponding FTE Worked Hours; the gap shows how much paid time is not spent working.

name: FTE Paid Hours - Distribution
definition: The size of the utility's distribution workforce expressed as full-time-equivalent (FTE) staff, based on hours paid. Calculated as total hours paid in distribution divided by the standard work hours of one full-time employee, which converts paid hours into an equivalent number of full-time staff. Higher values indicate a larger paid labour input to distribution. Because paid hours include annual leave, sick leave and public holidays, this measure normally sits above the corresponding FTE Worked Hours; the gap shows how much paid time is not spent working.

name: FTE Paid Hours - Other Electrical
definition: The size of the utility's other electrical activities workforce expressed as full-time-equivalent (FTE) staff, based on hours paid. Calculated as total hours paid in other electrical activities divided by the standard work hours of one full-time employee, which converts paid hours into an equivalent number of full-time staff. Higher values indicate a larger paid labour input to other electrical activities. Because paid hours include annual leave, sick leave and public holidays, this measure normally sits above the corresponding FTE Worked Hours; the gap shows how much paid time is not spent working.

name: FTE Paid Hours - Renewable Generation
definition: The size of the utility's renewable generation workforce expressed as full-time-equivalent (FTE) staff, based on hours paid. Calculated as total hours paid in renewable generation divided by the standard work hours of one full-time employee, which converts paid hours into an equivalent number of full-time staff. Higher values indicate a larger paid labour input to renewable generation. Because paid hours include annual leave, sick leave and public holidays, this measure normally sits above the corresponding FTE Worked Hours; the gap shows how much paid time is not spent working.

name: FTE Paid Hours - Transmission
definition: The size of the utility's transmission workforce expressed as full-time-equivalent (FTE) staff, based on hours paid. Calculated as total hours paid in transmission divided by the standard work hours of one full-time employee, which converts paid hours into an equivalent number of full-time staff. Higher values indicate a larger paid labour input to transmission. Because paid hours include annual leave, sick leave and public holidays, this measure normally sits above the corresponding FTE Worked Hours; the gap shows how much paid time is not spent working.

name: FTE Worked Hours - Conventional Generation
definition: The size of the utility's conventional (thermal) generation workforce expressed as full-time-equivalent (FTE) staff, based on hours actually worked. Calculated as total hours worked in conventional (thermal) generation divided by the standard work hours of one full-time employee, which converts raw hours into an equivalent number of full-time staff. Higher values indicate more labour effort applied to conventional (thermal) generation, whether from more staff or more overtime. Because it is built from worked hours it excludes leave and other paid non-working time; compare it with the corresponding FTE Paid Hours measure to see that gap.

name: FTE Worked Hours - Distribution
definition: The size of the utility's distribution workforce expressed as full-time-equivalent (FTE) staff, based on hours actually worked. Calculated as total hours worked in distribution divided by the standard work hours of one full-time employee, which converts raw hours into an equivalent number of full-time staff. Higher values indicate more labour effort applied to distribution, whether from more staff or more overtime. Because it is built from worked hours it excludes leave and other paid non-working time; compare it with the corresponding FTE Paid Hours measure to see that gap.

name: FTE Worked Hours - Other Electrical

Higher values indicate more labour effort applied to other electrical activities, whether from more staff or more overtime. name: FTE Worked Hours - Renewable Generation
definition: The size of the utility's renewable generation workforce expressed as full-time-equivalent (FTE) staff, based on hours actually worked. Calculated as total hours worked in renewable generation divided by the standard work hours of one full-time employee, which converts raw hours into an equivalent number of full-time staff. name: FTE Worked Hours - Transmission
definition: The size of the utility's transmission workforce expressed as full-time-equivalent (FTE) staff, based on hours actually worked. Calculated as total hours worked in transmission divided by the standard work hours of one full-time employee, which converts raw hours into an equivalent number of full-time staff. Higher values indicate more labour effort applied to transmission, whether from more staff or more overtime. Because it is built from worked hours it excludes leave and other paid non-working time; compare it with the corresponding FTE Paid Hours measure to see that gap.

name: Labor Productivity
definition: Measures workforce productivity as the number of customers served per employee. Calculated as the utility's total customer connections divided by its total number of employees. A higher value indicates each employee supports more customers, which generally signals a leaner, more productive workforce. Utilities serving many small, dispersed island grids naturally need more staff per customer, so comparisons are fairest between utilities of similar scale and geography.

name: Lost Time Injury Duration Rate
definition: Measures the amount of working time lost to work-related injuries, indicating how severe those injuries are; the source records the unit as incidents per million hours. Calculated as the hours lost to work-related injuries multiplied by eight and divided by the total number of employees. A lower value is better, indicating injuries cost less working time per employee. Note that the recorded unit does not match the per-employee formula, so confirm the intended basis before comparing across utilities.

name: Lost Time Injury Frequency Rate
definition: Measures how often work-related injuries occur relative to the hours the workforce actually works, expressed as incidents per million hours worked. Calculated as the number of work-related injuries divided by the sum of hours worked across conventional generation, renewable generation, network and other electrical functions, multiplied by one million. A lower rate is better, indicating fewer injuries for the labour effort expended. At small Pacific utilities a single injury can move the rate substantially, so multi-year trends are more informative than single-year values.
synonyms: injury frequency rate per million hours worked

name: Customer Consumption
definition: Measures the total volume of electricity sold to customers over the period, expressed in megawatt-hours (MWh). It is taken directly from the reported electricity sold to customers, i.e. metered and billed energy delivered. Higher values reflect a larger or more energy-intensive customer base; trends over time indicate demand growth or decline. Because it counts only billed energy, it excludes network losses and unbilled consumption, so it will always sit below energy sent out.

name: Customer Count
definition: Measures the total number of electricity customers served by the utility, expressed as a count of customers. It is taken directly from the reported number of metered customer connections. A higher or growing count indicates an expanding customer base and is the key denominator for per-customer KPIs such as SAIDI, SAIFI and consumption per customer. Note that it counts metered connections rather than people, so one connection may serve a multi-person household or a large commercial site.

name: Customers per Distribution Employee
definition: Measures distribution workforce productivity as the number of customers served per full-time-equivalent distribution employee. It is calculated by dividing the number of metered customer connections by the number of FTE employees working in the distribution function. A higher value indicates a leaner distribution operation relative to the customer base. Small island utilities naturally score lower because minimum staffing is needed regardless of scale, and outsourced distribution work can inflate the ratio without a true efficiency gain.

name: Distribution O&M Cost per km
definition: Measures the operations and maintenance cost intensity of the distribution network, expressed as cost per kilometre of network. It is calculated by dividing distribution O&M costs by the total length of the distribution network. A lower value suggests more cost-efficient network maintenance, though comparisons should allow for terrain, overhead versus underground construction and network age. A persistently very low value may indicate under-maintenance rather than efficiency, so it is best read alongside reliability KPIs.

name: Distribution Reliability
definition: Measures the fault rate of the distribution network, expressed as unplanned outage events per 100 kilometres of network. It is calculated by dividing the number of unplanned distribution network downtime events by the distribution network length and multiplying by 100. A lower value indicates a more reliable network with fewer faults per kilometre; a higher value points to asset condition, vegetation or weather exposure problems. Because it normalises by network length rather than customers affected, it complements rather than replaces SAIDI and SAIFI.

name: Network Delivery Losses
definition: Measures the share of energy entering the network that is lost before being billed to customers, expressed as a percentage. It is calculated as electricity generated minus station auxiliary usage minus electricity sold to customers, divided by electricity generated. A lower value is better: it means less energy is lost to technical causes (line and transformer losses) and non-technical causes (theft, metering and billing errors) combined. This KPI does not separate technical from non-technical losses, so a high figure warrants further investigation into which component dominates.

name: Transformer Utilization Factor
definition: Measures how heavily the utility's distribution transformer fleet is loaded, expressed as a percentage. It is calculated by dividing the average load on distribution transformers by the total installed transformer capacity. A higher value indicates better utilisation of transformer assets, while a very high value leaves little headroom for demand growth or contingencies; a low value suggests over-sized or under-used capacity. Because it uses average load, it can mask individual transformers that are overloaded at peak times.

name: Storage Efficiency
definition: Measures the round-trip efficiency of an energy storage system, expressed as a percentage. It is the ratio of energy discharged from the storage system to the energy supplied into it, with the shortfall lost in charging, conversion and standby. A higher value is better, meaning less energy is wasted for every unit cycled through the battery or other storage plant. Results depend on how the system is operated, so efficiencies are only strictly comparable over similar duty cycles.

name: Engine Oil Consumption
definition: Measures how much electricity is generated for each litre of engine fuel oil consumed by generators, expressed in kWh per litre. It relates the volume of oil supplied to generators to the electricity they generate over the same period. A higher value indicates more efficient conversion, i.e. more units generated per litre of oil; note that in kWh/litre form, higher is better, unlike litres-per-kWh measures where lower is better. Results vary with engine loading, so comparisons are most meaningful between similar duty cycles and machine types.

name: Generation Labor Productivity
definition: Measures the productivity of the generation workforce, expressed as megawatt-hours generated per full-time-equivalent generation employee. It is calculated by dividing total electricity generated by the number of FTE employees working in the generation function. A higher value indicates a leaner generation operation relative to output. Comparisons should allow for plant mix, since hydro and solar plants need far fewer operating staff per MWh than diesel stations, and for any outsourced O&M that removes staff from the count.

name: Generation O&M Costs per MWh
definition: Measures the operations and maintenance cost intensity of generation, expressed as cost per megawatt-hour generated. It is calculated by dividing generation O&M costs by total electricity generated. A lower value indicates more cost-efficient plant operation, though fuel type, plant age and unit size strongly influence achievable levels. A very low value sustained over several years can signal deferred maintenance rather than genuine efficiency, so it should be read alongside availability and forced outage KPIs.

name: Generator Availability Factor
definition: Measures the share of hours in the period during which generating plant was available to run, expressed as a percentage. It is calculated by subtracting planned and unplanned downtime hours from the total hours in the period and dividing the result by the total hours in the period. A higher value is better, indicating plant is ready to generate when needed; unlike capacity factor, it measures readiness to run rather than actual output, so a plant can be highly available but lightly used. Low availability points to excessive maintenance outages or forced outages and should be read with the planned and forced outage indicators.

name: Generator Capacity Factor
definition: Measures actual electricity generated as a share of the maximum that could have been generated if the plant had run at full installed capacity for the whole period, expressed as a percentage. It is calculated by dividing electricity generated by the energy equivalent of installed capacity over the period. A higher value indicates fuller utilisation of installed plant; unlike availability factor, it reflects how much the plant actually ran, not merely whether it was ready to run. Low capacity factors are normal for peaking and standby units and for variable renewables, so comparisons should be made within plant types.

name: Generator Forced Outage Indicator
definition: Measures the share of potential generator operating hours lost to unplanned (forced) outages, expressed as a percentage. It is calculated by dividing total unplanned downtime hours by the total hours in the period multiplied by the number of active generators. A lower value is better: forced outages are unexpected failures, so a high value signals poor plant condition, maintenance quality or fuel problems. It complements the planned outage indicator, which covers scheduled maintenance downtime instead.

name: Generator Planned Outage Indicator
definition: Measures the share of potential generator operating hours lost to planned outages such as scheduled maintenance and overhauls, expressed as a percentage. It is calculated by dividing total planned downtime hours by the total hours in the period multiplied by the number of active generators. A lower value means less plant time committed to scheduled work, but very low values over several years may indicate maintenance is being deferred rather than avoided. It complements the forced outage indicator, which captures unexpected failures.

name: IPP Generation
definition: Measures the share of total grid electricity that is generated by independent power producers (IPPs) rather than by the utility's own plant, expressed as a percentage. It is calculated by dividing electricity generated by IPPs by total electricity generated from all sources. A higher value indicates greater reliance on purchased power, which shifts the utility's cost structure from fuel and O&M towards power purchase agreements. It is a structural indicator rather than a good/bad measure, but it is essential context when comparing generation cost and efficiency KPIs.

name: Load Factor
definition: Measures how evenly electricity demand is spread over the period, expressed as a percentage. It is calculated by dividing average load by peak load. A higher value indicates a flatter demand profile, meaning generation and network assets sized for the peak are used more fully throughout the day and year; a low value means capacity sits idle outside short peaks. Note the distinction from capacity factor: load factor describes the shape of demand, whereas capacity factor describes how hard the generating plant actually ran.

name: Lubrication Oil Consumption
definition: Measures how much electricity is generated for each litre of lubrication oil consumed, expressed in kWh per litre. It is calculated by dividing electricity generated by the volume of lubricating oil used, scaled by 1,000 to convert to kWh per litre. A higher value is better, indicating engines are consuming less lube oil per unit generated; a falling trend often gives early warning of engine wear, ring or seal problems. Comparisons are most meaningful between similar engine types and duty cycles.
synonyms: kWh per litre of lube oil

name: Renewable Energy to Grid
definition: Measures the share of grid electricity supplied from renewable sources such as hydro, solar, wind and biomass, expressed as a percentage. It is calculated by dividing electricity generated from renewable sources by total electricity generated from all sources. A higher value indicates lower dependence on imported fossil fuel and progress towards national renewable energy targets. High shares of variable renewables can, however, increase the need for storage and grid stability measures, so the figure is best read alongside reliability KPIs.

name: Station Usage/Station Auxiliaries
definition: Measures the share of generated electricity consumed by the power station itself, expressed as a percentage. It is calculated by dividing station auxiliary usage — energy used for pumps, fans, cooling, fuel handling, lighting and other in-station loads — by total electricity generated. A lower value is better, since energy used within the station is not available for sale. Persistently high station usage points to inefficient auxiliary plant or units running at poor load points.

name: Planned SAIDI
definition: Measures the average duration of planned supply interruptions experienced by customers over the year, expressed in minutes per customer. It is calculated by dividing the total customer-minutes of planned interruptions by the number of customers affected by those interruptions. A lower value is better, indicating that scheduled work such as maintenance and connections is completed with less supply-off time per customer; momentary interruptions of under one minute are excluded. Note that dividing by customers affected, rather than total customers served as in the classic SAIDI convention, makes this closer to an average outage duration for affected customers, so treat cross-utility comparisons with care.
synonyms: planned System Average Interruption Duration Index

name: Planned SAIFI
definition: Measures how often customers experience planned supply interruptions over the year, expressed as interruption events per customer. It is calculated by dividing the total number of planned interruption events by the number of customers affected by those interruptions. A lower value is better, indicating scheduled work is bundled efficiently so customers are interrupted less often; momentary interruptions of under one minute are excluded. Note that dividing by customers affected, rather than total customers served as in the classic SAIFI convention, alters the result, so treat cross-utility comparisons with care.
synonyms: planned System Average Interruption Frequency Index

name: Unplanned SAIDI
definition: Measures the average total duration of unplanned (forced) supply interruptions per customer served per year, expressed in minutes per customer. Following the standard SAIDI convention, it is the sum of customer-minutes of sustained unplanned interruptions divided by the total number of customers served, with momentary interruptions of under one minute excluded. A lower value is better, indicating customers lose supply for less time due to faults, equipment failures and weather events. It is the headline network reliability measure and is best read alongside unplanned SAIFI to distinguish long-but-rare from short-but-frequent outages.
synonyms: unplanned System Average Interruption Duration Index

name: Unplanned SAIFI
definition: Measures how often the average customer experiences an unplanned (forced) sustained supply interruption per year, expressed as interruption events per customer. Following the standard SAIFI convention, it is the total number of sustained unplanned customer interruptions divided by the total number of customers served, with momentary interruptions of under one minute excluded. A lower value is better, indicating faults and failures interrupt customers less frequently. Read together with unplanned SAIDI: SAIFI shows how often outages occur, SAIDI shows how long they last in total.
synonyms: unplanned System Average Interruption Frequency Index

name: Transmission Network Losses
definition: Measures the share of energy entering the transmission network that is lost before delivery, expressed as a percentage. It is calculated as electricity sent out (generation less station auxiliary usage) minus energy delivered from transmission and energy sold to customers, divided by electricity sent out. A lower value is better, indicating less energy dissipated in transmission lines and substation transformers; transmission losses are predominantly technical rather than theft-related. Comparisons should allow for network length, voltage levels and load, which strongly influence achievable loss levels.

name: Transmission Reliability
definition: Measures the outage rate of the transmission network, expressed as outage events per 100 kilometres of network. It is calculated by adding planned and unplanned transmission network downtime events, dividing by transmission network length, and multiplying by 100. A lower value indicates a more reliable transmission system with fewer outages per kilometre. Because it combines planned and unplanned events, a high value may reflect a heavy maintenance programme rather than poor asset condition, so it is best read with the planned and unplanned transmission SAIDI/SAIFI measures.

name: Transmission SAIDI Planned
definition: Measures the average duration of planned supply interruptions originating in the transmission network, expressed in minutes per customer per year. Following the SAIDI convention, it is the total customer-minutes of sustained planned transmission-caused interruptions divided by customers served, with momentary interruptions of under one minute excluded. A lower value is better, indicating scheduled transmission work is carried out with less customer supply-off time. Because single transmission outages can affect very large numbers of customers, one major planned outage can dominate the annual figure.
synonyms: planned transmission minutes lost per customer

name: Transmission SAIDI Unplanned
definition: Measures the average duration of unplanned (forced) supply interruptions originating in the transmission network, expressed in minutes per customer per year. Following the SAIDI convention, it is the total customer-minutes of sustained unplanned transmission-caused interruptions divided by customers served, with momentary interruptions of under one minute excluded. A lower value is better, indicating transmission faults cost customers less supply-off time. Transmission events are rarer than distribution faults but affect many customers at once, so this measure can be volatile from year to year.
synonyms: transmission fault minutes lost per customer

name: Transmission SAIFI Planned
definition: Measures how often customers experience planned supply interruptions originating in the transmission network, expressed as interruption events per customer per year. Following the SAIFI convention, it is the total number of sustained planned transmission-caused customer interruptions divided by customers served, with momentary interruptions of under one minute excluded. A lower value is better, indicating scheduled transmission work interrupts customers less often. Values are typically much lower than distribution SAIFI because transmission outages are less frequent, though each affects many customers.

name: Transmission SAIFI Unplanned
definition: Measures how often customers experience unplanned (forced) supply interruptions originating in the transmission network, expressed as interruption events per customer per year. Following the SAIFI convention, it is the total number of sustained unplanned transmission-caused customer interruptions divided by customers served, with momentary interruptions of under one minute excluded. A lower value is better, indicating transmission faults interrupt customers less frequently. Because single transmission events can interrupt a large share of all customers simultaneously, one severe event can dominate the annual figure.
